Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Advanced Data Governance Features

Advanced Data Governance Features

Protect sensitive columns, restrict row visibility, and tag objects for governance and cost attribution without moving or copying data.

In this lesson
Understand masking, row access, and tagging with live SQL examples, tests, and best practices to avoid common mistakes.
Why it matters
Meet compliance needs while enabling analytics by protecting PII and enforcing tenant isolation at query time.
Explore Key Topics
Dynamic Data Masking
Mask column values by role so one table serves many audiences.
Row Access Policies
Filter rows at query time to enforce tenant and regional isolation.
Object Tagging
Assign key-value tags for classification, discovery, and cost allocation.
Visual summary
Masking
Transforms column values at query time.
Row Access
Filters rows using user or role context.
Quick note
Using these features together gives you layered protection. Masking controls values, row policies control visibility, and tags support identification and billing. Plan mapping tables and role grants carefully to avoid accidental denials or performance issues.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical testing and common pitfalls. Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Practical Skills

Practical Skills and Tests

Concrete checks that prove your policies work and won't disrupt production.

Grants & Ownership
Apply policies from the owning role or grant APPLY privileges to the owner. Avoid using ACCOUNTADMIN for routine application to keep least privilege.
Testing with Roles
Switch roles and run SELECTs to confirm different masked outputs and row visibility. Use mapping table rows to validate row filters.
Common Mistakes
Overly complex policy logic, incomplete mapping tables, and applying policies from non-owning roles can cause unexpected denials or performance issues.
Quick checklist
  • Grant CREATE and APPLY privileges correctly.
  • Test with at least two roles.
  • Keep mapping queries efficient.
  • Standardize tags for discovery.

screens.title: Masking vs Row Access vs Tagging
screens.narratorSegment: Let's clarify the fundamental differences so you choose the right control. Dynamic data masking changes the representation of column values when a query runs; it does not remove rows or change stored data. Use masking when columns contain PII or sensitive fields that certain roles should not see in full—for example, show analysts only the last four digits of an SSN while security officers see the full value. Row access policies are used when entire rows must be hidden from certain users: multi-tenant datasets, regional data isolation, or salesperson-only views. If a user should never see rows for other tenants, use a row access policy that checks their region or tenant mapping. Object tagging is orthogonal: it doesn't change visibility but labels objects for classification, discovery, and cost reports. Tags help you find all columns marked PII or track warehouse spend by project. A common misconception is using row policies to hide columns or masks to restrict rows; these produce incorrect outcomes. Decide by asking: is the sensitivity at the value level or the entire record level? That question points to masking or row filtering respectively. A short practice: imagine a transactions table—mask credit card numbers, but use row policies to limit which account holders a rep may see.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Masking vs Row Access vs Tagging
Comparison

Use the rule: value-level sensitivity → masking. record-level access → row policy. classification/metadata → tags.

Dynamic Data Masking
  • Masks column values dynamically.
  • Same table, different outputs per role.
  • Good for PII like SSN or credit cards.
Row Access Policies
  • Filters which rows are returned.
  • Essential for multi-tenant isolation.
  • Depends on user/role or mapping tables.
Object Tagging
  • Key-value metadata on objects.
  • Used for discovery, compliance, and cost attribution.
  • Does not alter query results by itself.
Example
In a transactions table, mask credit card numbers for analysts while using a row policy to limit reps to their region's rows.
Key Takeaway
Pick the control matching the unit of protection: value vs record vs metadata.
Common Mistake

Avoid using masking to limit rows or tags to imply access control. Each feature serves a distinct purpose and mixing them without design leads to gaps.

Try this
Sketch a quick decision rule for your dataset: which columns are PII, which records are tenant-specific, and which objects need tags for billing.

screens.title: Dynamic Data Masking — Concept and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic data masking lets you present different views of the same stored value depending on the querying user's role or attributes. The underlying data remains unmodified in storage; masking only affects the returned result set. This is powerful because teams can avoid making redacted copies of tables and still comply with privacy rules. Typical use cases include social security numbers, credit card numbers, or email addresses where some roles need the full value and others need a partially redacted or NULL value. Implementing a masking policy usually centers on CURRENT_ROLE() or other session context to decide which mask to apply. A practical example: allow SECURITY_OFFICER to see full SSNs, DATA_ANALYST to see only the last four digits, and everyone else to see asterisks. Be mindful of performance: overly complex masks that call heavy functions can slow queries. Also test policy logic with all relevant roles so you do not accidentally leak data to an unexpected role. After you define a clear mask, apply it to the column and validate with targeted SELECTs under multiple roles to confirm behavior. Dynamic Data Masking — Concept and Use Cases means masking controls representation per role; it protects values while keeping one canonical dataset for all users.. In practical terms, how masking preserves a single source of truth while protecting values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Dynamic Data Masking
What it is

A masking policy returns obfuscated values at query time based on role or session context while underlying data remains unchanged.

Why use it
  • Maintains one canonical dataset for all consumers.
  • Reduces data duplication and simplifies governance.
  • Supports granular exposure rules by role.
Concrete example
Show analysts only the last four digits of SSNs while security officers see the full number. No separate redacted table needed.
Common mistake
Not testing policies with every relevant role or creating overly complex logic that hurts query performance.
Example Masking Policy (reference)
CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY ssn_mask_policy AS (val VARCHAR) RETURNS VARCHAR ->
  CASE
    WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SECURITY_OFFICER' THEN val
    WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() = 'DATA_ANALYST' THEN '***-**-' || SUBSTR(val,7,4)
    ELSE '********'
  END;
Apply and test
After creating the policy, ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... SET MASKING POLICY and then SELECT the column while switching roles to confirm results.

screens.title: Create and Apply a Masking Policy — Live Code
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through the exact S Q L used to create and apply a masking policy. The first statement defines the policy logic: it accepts the column value and returns either the full value, a truncated form, or a masked string depending on the current role. After creating the policy, you must apply it to the target column using ALTER TABLE... MODIFY COLUMN... SET MASKING POLICY. Test by switching roles and running the same SELECT to observe different outputs. Pay attention to privileges: the role running CREATE MASKING POLICY needs that privilege, and the role applying the policy needs APPLY MASKING POLICY and ownership on the table. A common error is applying a policy from a role that does not own the table or failing to grant APPLY privileges, which can lead to confusion about why the mask does not take effect. Also avoid embedding expensive expressions inside the policy. Keep masks simple and test performance on representative queries before deploying widely. Finally, validate results for analyst and security roles so you can demonstrate expected behavior. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Masking Policy Code Walkthrough
Create and attach a masking policy

This example matches the chapter source. Run as a role with the required privileges and then apply to the SSN column.

-- Create a masking policy
CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY ssn_mask_policy AS (val VARCHAR) RETURNS VARCHAR ->
    CASE
        WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SECURITY_OFFICER' THEN val
        WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() = 'DATA_ANALYST' THEN '***-**-' || SUBSTR(val, 7, 4)
        ELSE '********'
    END;

-- Apply to column (role must have APPLY MASKING POLICY and ownership)
ALTER TABLE customer_info MODIFY COLUMN ssn SET MASKING POLICY ssn_mask_policy;
Testing steps
  1. USE ROLE data_analyst; SELECT customer_id, customer_name, ssn FROM customer_info; confirm masked output.
  2. USE ROLE security_officer; run the same SELECT; confirm full SSNs.
  3. If results differ, check APPLY privileges and table ownership.
Pro tip
Keep masking logic simple and predictable. Use CURRENT_ROLE() checks when roles are well-defined, or session attributes for more dynamic rules.
Pitfall
Complex subqueries or nested functions inside the mask can increase query cost. Test with realistic queries before rollout.

screens.title: Row Access Policies — Concept and Mapping Tables
screens.narratorSegment: Row access policies let you define boolean logic that determines whether a row is visible to the querying session. Unlike masking, which changes values, row access policies filter entire rows. They are ideal for multi-tenant or regional isolation: only rows that match the user's tenant or region mapping are returned. Common implementations use a mapping table that pairs CURRENT_USER() with permitted regions or tenants. A typical pattern allows admin roles to bypass the filter and returns true for them, while regular users are checked against the mapping table with an EXISTS subquery. Be careful: the mapping table must be kept up to date and indexed appropriately; otherwise, you risk denying access to authorized users. Performance is another consideration—inefficient subqueries inside row policies can slow many queries. Always test row access logic with representative workloads and maintain clarity in the mapping data to avoid accidental data hiding. Row Access Policies — Concept and Mapping Tables means row access policies are boolean filters that hide entire rows unless a user's role or mapping entry permits them.. In practical terms, filter which rows a user may see by role or mapping table membership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Row Access Policies
Why row access policies

They enforce which rows a user can read without duplicating data or creating separate tables for each tenant or region.

Pattern
  • Use mapping tables to relate CURRENT_USER() to permitted regions or tenants.
  • Allow admin roles to bypass filters for management tasks.
  • Keep policy logic simple to reduce query overhead.
Concrete scenario
A sales representative should only see rows whose sales_region matches their assigned region in user_regions. Managers see all rows.
Example Row Access Policy (reference)
CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY region_access_policy
AS (region_id VARCHAR) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
    CURRENT_ROLE() IN ('ACCOUNTADMIN','SECURITY_ADMIN')
    OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM user_regions WHERE user_name = CURRENT_USER() AND region = region_id
    );

ALTER TABLE sales ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY region_access_policy ON (sales_region_id);

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Row Access Policy Code Walkthrough
Mapping table and policy

Create user_regions, insert mappings, then create and attach the row access policy to customer_info on region.

-- Create mapping table
CREATE TABLE user_regions (user_name VARCHAR, region VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO user_regions VALUES ('your_user', 'East');

-- Create row access policy
CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY region_filter_policy
AS (customer_region VARCHAR) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
    CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SECURITY_OFFICER'
    OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM user_regions WHERE user_name = CURRENT_USER() AND region = customer_region
    );

-- Attach to table
ALTER TABLE customer_info ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY region_filter_policy ON (region);
Validation
USE ROLE data_analyst; SELECT * FROM customer_info; should return only East rows. USE ROLE security_officer; SELECT * FROM customer_info; should return all rows.
Checklist
  • Is the mapping table populated and current?
  • Does the policy reference the correct column?
  • Does the applying role have APPLY ROW ACCESS POLICY and ownership?

screens.title: Testing, Common Pitfalls, and Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Testing policies thoroughly is essential. For masking, switch roles and run the same SELECT to compare outputs; this shows whether the applied mask returns correct values. For row policies, test with users who should and should not see certain rows, and verify mapping table entries match CURRENT_USER() values. Common pitfalls include incomplete or stale mapping entries, policy logic that is too permissive or too restrictive, and applying policies from roles without proper ownership which may leave the policy inactive. Performance problems often arise when policies run subqueries or complex functions per row; these add overhead to many queries. To mitigate this, keep policy logic simple, avoid heavy aggregations inside policy code, and consider precomputing mappings or using efficient lookups. Another approach is to measure impact in a staging environment by running representative queries before and after attaching a policy. Finally, document policies and maintain a small test suite of role-switch queries so you can detect regressions quickly when changes are made. Testing, Common Pitfalls, and Performance Considerations means always validate with role-switch tests, keep policies simple, and measure query impact in staging before production rollout.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore three native Snowflake features that let you protect and classify data without creating extra copies. You will learn what dynamic data masking does, how row access policies filter rows, and how object tags make classification and cost attribution consistent across objects. These mechanisms let teams apply the right visibility and metadata where needed: masking controls what values a user sees in a column, row access limits which rows a user may read, and tags let you categorize objects for compliance and billing. We'll use concrete S Q L examples that create and apply a masking policy and a row access policy, then test results with roles like DATA_ANALYST and SECURITY_OFFICER. You'll also see how to create tags and attach them to warehouses, tables, and columns to support discovery and reporting. By the end, you'll understand when to use each feature, how they interact, and common mistakes to avoid so your policies are effective and maintainable. Consider how these tools could reduce the need for separate redacted tables and support auditability in your environment.

These learning objectives make the chapter actionable. First, you will implement dynamic data masking policies so sensitive columns display masked values for some roles and full values for others. That skill is useful when you want one canonical table to serve multiple audiences without creating redacted copies. Second, you'll configure row access policies to control row-level visibility using role and user attributes; this is essential for multi-tenant data separation and regional restrictions. Third, you will understand object tagging for classification and cost attribution so teams can find PII and track spending by project. Fourth, you'll practice differentiating masking and row policies and choosing the correct feature for a requirement. Each objective includes hands-on S Q L and testing steps so you can verify behavior with example roles like DATA_ANALYST and SECURITY_OFFICER. By the end you will also apply best practices for integrating these features into a live Snowflake environment, including grant and ownership considerations to avoid common mistakes that hide data or cause performance regressions.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical testing and common pitfalls. You will practice granting the correct privileges: CREATE MASKING POLICY and APPLY MASKING POLICY for masking, CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY and APPLY ROW ACCESS POLICY for row filters, and CREATE TAG for tags. We emphasize ownership: apply policies from the role that owns the table or grant APPLY privileges to the owning role instead of using ACCOUNTADMIN for routine configuration. You'll also learn how to test: switch roles and run the same SELECT to observe differences, and validate mapping tables used by row policies. Another goal is to recognize common mistakes: overly complex policy logic that slows queries, mapping tables that are incomplete or mismatched to CURRENT_USER(), and inconsistent tagging. Each objective includes a verification step so you can demonstrate competency: create the policy, apply it, and show expected results for at least two roles. Practicing these steps reduces surprises in production and helps you meet compliance goals without disrupting analytics workloads.

Let's clarify the fundamental differences so you choose the right control. Dynamic data masking changes the representation of column values when a query runs; it does not remove rows or change stored data. Use masking when columns contain PII or sensitive fields that certain roles should not see in full—for example, show analysts only the last four digits of an SSN while security officers see the full value. Row access policies are used when entire rows must be hidden from certain users: multi-tenant datasets, regional data isolation, or salesperson-only views. If a user should never see rows for other tenants, use a row access policy that checks their region or tenant mapping. Object tagging is orthogonal: it doesn't change visibility but labels objects for classification, discovery, and cost reports. Tags help you find all columns marked PII or track warehouse spend by project. A common misconception is using row policies to hide columns or masks to restrict rows; these produce incorrect outcomes. Decide by asking: is the sensitivity at the value level or the entire record level? That question points to masking or row filtering respectively. A short practice: imagine a transactions table—mask credit card numbers, but use row policies to limit which account holders a rep may see.

Dynamic data masking lets you present different views of the same stored value depending on the querying user's role or attributes. The underlying data remains unmodified in storage; masking only affects the returned result set. This is powerful because teams can avoid making redacted copies of tables and still comply with privacy rules. Typical use cases include social security numbers, credit card numbers, or email addresses where some roles need the full value and others need a partially redacted or NULL value. Implementing a masking policy usually centers on CURRENT_ROLE() or other session context to decide which mask to apply. A practical example: allow SECURITY_OFFICER to see full SSNs, DATA_ANALYST to see only the last four digits, and everyone else to see asterisks. Be mindful of performance: overly complex masks that call heavy functions can slow queries. Also test policy logic with all relevant roles so you do not accidentally leak data to an unexpected role. After you define a clear mask, apply it to the column and validate with targeted SELECTs under multiple roles to confirm behavior. Dynamic Data Masking — Concept and Use Cases means masking controls representation per role; it protects values while keeping one canonical dataset for all users.. In practical terms, how masking preserves a single source of truth while protecting values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we'll walk through the exact S Q L used to create and apply a masking policy. The first statement defines the policy logic: it accepts the column value and returns either the full value, a truncated form, or a masked string depending on the current role. After creating the policy, you must apply it to the target column using ALTER TABLE... MODIFY COLUMN... SET MASKING POLICY. Test by switching roles and running the same SELECT to observe different outputs. Pay attention to privileges: the role running CREATE MASKING POLICY needs that privilege, and the role applying the policy needs APPLY MASKING POLICY and ownership on the table. A common error is applying a policy from a role that does not own the table or failing to grant APPLY privileges, which can lead to confusion about why the mask does not take effect. Also avoid embedding expensive expressions inside the policy. Keep masks simple and test performance on representative queries before deploying widely. Finally, validate results for analyst and security roles so you can demonstrate expected behavior. Row access policies let you define boolean logic that determines whether a row is visible to the querying session. Unlike masking, which changes values, row access policies filter entire rows. They are ideal for multi-tenant or regional isolation: only rows that match the user's tenant or region mapping are returned. Common implementations use a mapping table that pairs CURRENT_USER() with permitted regions or tenants. A typical pattern allows admin roles to bypass the filter and returns true for them, while regular users are checked against the mapping table with an EXISTS subquery. Be careful: the mapping table must be kept up to date and indexed appropriately; otherwise, you risk denying access to authorized users. Performance is another consideration—inefficient subqueries inside row policies can slow many queries. Always test row access logic with representative workloads and maintain clarity in the mapping data to avoid accidental data hiding. Then define the row access policy to allow admin roles and otherwise check the mapping with EXISTS. Finally, attach the policy with ALTER TABLE... ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY on the region column. For row policies, test with users who should and should not see certain rows, and verify mapping table entries match CURRENT_USER() values. Object tagging attaches key-value metadata to Snowflake objects so you can classify data and attribute costs. Let's summarize the essential ideas. Dynamic data masking changes how column values are presented to users at query time based on role or context while preserving the underlying stored data. Masking policies are applied to columns and should be tested across roles. Row access policies filter which rows are returned, using role checks or mapping tables to enforce tenant or regional isolation. Object tagging attaches searchable key-value metadata to Snowflake objects for classification, discovery, and cost attribution; tags do not change access by themselves. Together, these tools form a layered governance approach: masks for value-level protection, row policies for record-level isolation, and tags to support discovery and reporting. Remember to standardize tags, keep policy logic simple, and automate testing so your governance controls are reliable and auditable.
